analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve major federal regulations before they can take effect.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 241-184 on December 7, 2011, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died in committee when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a major federal rule takes effect unless both chambers of Congress vote to cancel it. This bill flips that default: any rule the government estimates will cost the economy $100 million or more per year, or significantly raise prices or hurt jobs and investment, could not take effect unless both chambers pass a resolution approving it and the President signs it. Because Congress rarely agrees on anything, most major rules would simply die by default unless Congress affirmatively acted within 70 working days. That would apply to big clean air, food safety, workplace safety, and financial rules, among many others. The bill passed the House but never got a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Large regulated businesses and their trade associations gain the most: any major rule they opposed could be killed simply by Congress doing nothing. Members of Congress would also gain formal power over executive branch decisions, which the bill's sponsors framed as restoring accountability for laws Congress passes in vague form.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries and business trade groups

how_it_helps.text: A 'major rule' — one with $100 million or more in annual economic effects, a major increase in costs or prices, or significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, or productivity — could not take effect unless Congress enacted a joint resolution approving it.
If no approval resolution was signed into law within 70 session days or legislative days after the agency reported the rule, the rule would be deemed not approved and would never take effect.
The approval resolutions could not be amended, and Senate procedures forced a vote within tight deadlines, so opponents of a rule would get an up-or-down vote they could otherwise never obtain.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal protections would bear the cost. Clean air and water limits, food safety standards, workplace safety rules, consumer financial protections, and similar safeguards that meet the $100 million threshold would be blocked by default whenever Congress declined or failed to act — which, given the difficulty of passing legislation, would be most of the time.
analysis.who_pays_short: People protected by federal safety and health rules

drawbacks.text: Rules covering areas like air pollution, food safety, and financial protection would be blocked by default, because each would need an affirmative act of both chambers plus a presidential signature within 70 session days, and even a supportive Congress could not realistically approve the hundreds of rules that meet the threshold.

The emergency escape valve was narrow: a President could let a major rule take effect for one 90-day period only for an imminent health or safety threat, criminal enforcement, national security, or trade agreement implementation.

Supporters' good-faith argument was accountability: Congress passes laws in broad strokes and unelected agency staff fill in costly details, so requiring a recorded vote would force lawmakers to own the rules made in their name.

An attempt to add country-of-origin labeling protections for food safety and consumers' right to know was rejected when a motion to recommit the bill with those instructions failed 183-235, with nearly all Republicans voting no.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability concern is legitimate: Congress does delegate broad rulemaking power, and a vote requirement would make members answerable for major rules. But the design goes far beyond forcing deliberation. With a default death sentence, no amendments allowed, and a 70-working-day clock, the bill would function as a near-blanket stop on major rulemaking whenever the chambers disagreed or simply did nothing — and the cost would land on the people the rules protect, while the businesses being regulated would gain a quiet way to block rules without ever having to argue against them on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill on December 7, 2011, but the Senate's Homeland Security committee never acted on it, so it never came to a Senate vote before Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill as amended in November 2011 after a 22-14 committee vote, and the Rules Committee then reported a rule for floor consideration.
On final passage the bill was approved 241-184, with 237 of 241 voting Republicans in favor and only 4 of 192 voting Democrats.
A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to add country-of-origin food labeling failed 183-235, with 181 of 192 Democrats in favor and all but 2 of 241 Republicans opposed.
The Senate received the bill on December 8, 2011, and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on major federal health, safety, and financial protections kept them, because the Senate never acted. The regulated industries that would have gained a default veto over major rules did not get it.

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 237 of 241 voting Republicans supported the bill while only 4 of 192 voting Democrats did; the same split appeared on the failed motion to recommit, which 181 of 192 Democrats backed and all but 2 Republicans opposed.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturers, energy, chemical, and financial firms)
industries.note: The bill would have given any business facing a major rule a default win: if Congress failed to pass an approval resolution in 70 working days, the rule died without a vote on its merits. The industry's gain — relief from costly standards — is the public's loss of the protections those standards provide.

industries.industry: Business trade associations and lobbying firms
industries.note: Stopping a major rule would no longer require persuading Congress to pass a disapproval resolution and override a president; it would only require preventing an approval resolution, a far easier lobbying task. That shifts leverage toward organized interests over diffuse public benefits.

Agencies would lose the ability to put major rules into effect on their own, since no rule above the $100 million threshold could take effect without an enacted joint resolution. The public shares this loss when agency inaction means unaddressed hazards.

An amendment to require country-of-origin labeling for meat and food, protecting consumers' right to know where food comes from, was rejected during floor consideration. Most in the sector opposed such labeling requirements, and the bill's framework would have made new labeling rules above the threshold especially hard to enact.
